questions.prompt: How many valence electrons does an alkali metal atom have?
questions.explanation: Every alkali metal has exactly one valence electron — the single outer electron that drives the whole family's behavior.
questions.misconception: Seven is the halogens' valence count and eight is the noble gases' — the alkali metals are the one-electron family, which is precisely what makes them so eager to react.

questions.prompt: Why do alkali metals react so violently, for example with water?
options: They lose their one outer electron very easily and fast
They have full outer shells to protect
questions.explanation: Losing a single outer electron is easy and fast, leaving a stable full shell — so the reaction happens violently, releasing heat and gas.
questions.misconception: Weight and temperature have nothing to do with it — the speed comes from how easy it is to shed that one lonely valence electron.

questions.prompt: When an alkali metal like sodium reacts, what does it become?
options: A +1 ion (Na⁺) after losing one electron
A -1 ion after gaining an electron
questions.explanation: Sodium loses its one valence electron and becomes a +1 cation, Na⁺ — with a full, stable shell left behind.
questions.misconception: Alkali metals give electrons away, they don't grab them — so they become positive +1 ions, the exact opposite of gaining a negative charge.

questions.prompt: Which group of the periodic table are the alkali metals?
questions.explanation: The alkali metals occupy Group 1 — the first column at the far left of the periodic table.
questions.misconception: The far right (Group 18) holds the noble gases and Group 17 holds the halogens — the alkali metals specifically own that first left-hand column.
